terroir.climate: Mediterranean, with wet winters and warm, dry summers, moderated by the sea. False Bay lies fifteen kilometres south of the town, and its breezes reach the Helderberg and the southern farms every afternoon; the Cape Doctor, the dry south-easter of summer, blows hard across the district, drying the canopy and holding off rot at the cost of some wind damage. Sites range from warm valley floors to cool upper slopes at 400 metres and more, so a single district holds early-picked Sauvignon Blanc and slow-ripening Cabernet.
terroir.soils: Decomposed granite on the foot slopes of the Simonsberg, the Helderberg and the Stellenbosch Mountain: a reddish, clay-bearing loam that holds water through the dry summer and gives the district's structured Cabernet. Table Mountain sandstone higher up, weathering to pale, hungry, sandy soils that suit white grapes. Malmesbury shale on the lower hills to the west, in the Bottelary and Devon Valley, giving softer, rounder reds. Alluvial sand and gravel along the Eerste River and towards False Bay.
terroir.topography: A bowl of valleys and hills between three mountains: the Simonsberg to the north, the Jonkershoek range and Stellenbosch Mountain to the east, the Helderberg to the south above Somerset West. The Bottelary hills and the Polkadraai hills roll westward towards the Cape Flats, lower and warmer. Aspect matters: much of the best Cabernet sits on south- and south-west-facing foot slopes, open to the afternoon sea breeze.
terroir.water: The Eerste River rises in the Jonkershoek valley and runs through the town to False Bay. The bay itself is the district's cooling engine, carrying Indian Ocean air inland each afternoon; the Atlantic, on the far side of the peninsula, matters less here than it does at Constantia and Darling.

traps: The Simonsberg has two wards: Simonsberg-Stellenbosch on this side and Simonsberg-Paarl on the Paarl side.
Helderberg appears on wine lists and in conversation but is not a Wine of Origin ward; its wines are labelled Stellenbosch.
Pinotage's second parent is Cinsaut, then called Hermitage; it is not Syrah, whatever the Rhône hill suggests.
The first Pinotage was crossed in 1925 but not sold until 1961; the dates are thirty six years apart.
Cape Blend has no legal definition; the rule of thumb of a third to two thirds Pinotage is the trade's, not the law's.
Stellenbosch is a district, so a blend with Paarl fruit must drop to Coastal Region; the Western Cape on a label is the geographical unit, not a sign of lesser quality.
Vlottenburg is the eighth ward, from 2020; older lists give seven.

wines.note: Deep, cassis-and-cedar reds with graphite, dried herb and a firm tannin that needs five years and rewards fifteen; decant, serve at cellar temperature, pair with beef, lamb or venison.

Cabernet Sauvignon led with Merlot and Cabernet Franc, sometimes Petit Verdot; the Cape's grandest red category, with Paul Sauer and Rubicon as its two benchmarks. Cigar box, cassis and a long, dry finish.
Mulberry, plum and smoke with a savoury, sometimes tarry grip from old bush vines; the best are fermented in open concrete vats and aged in oak. Serve with game, barbecue and spiced lamb.
A red blend built on Pinotage with Cabernet, Merlot or Shiraz; a trade category rather than a law, usually with Pinotage at between a third and two thirds of the blend.
Barrel-fermented, textured and dry, with quince, pear and honey over fresh acidity; the serious face of the Cape's most planted grape, good with pork, poultry and rich fish.
Pungent, flinty Sauvignon from the higher and cooler farms, and barrel-fermented Chardonnay from the Simonsberg and Banghoek; the whites a server pours most by the glass.
Bottle-fermented sparkling wine from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, a category born here in 1971 and made by several of the district's estates.

exam: Swartland against Stellenbosch: dry-farmed bush vines, Syrah and Rhône blends and old Chenin on granite and shale, against trellised Cabernet on the mountain slopes near False Bay.
Columella and Palladius by name: a Syrah-led red blend and a Chenin-led white blend from Sadie Family Wines at Malmesbury.
The two soils, granite on the Paardeberg and shale or schist around Riebeek and Porseleinberg, and what each does to Syrah.
The Swartland Independent Producers charter of 2010: Swartland fruit, native yeasts, no acid or tannin additions, little new oak; a seal, not a law.
The Old Vine Project seal: thirty five years, planting date on the label, from 2018.
The wards by name, Malmesbury, Riebeekberg, Riebeeksrivier, Paardeberg, Paardeberg South, Porseleinberg and Piket-Bo-Berg, and Darling as a separate district since 2003.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The red that made the district's name: peppery, savoury, scented with fynbos and dried herb, firm but not heavy, fermented with whole bunches and aged in old wood, alone or leading a Rhône-style blend.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: Old dry-farmed bush vines give concentrated, textured, honeyed whites with quince, straw and a saline finish, fermented in old barrels or concrete rather than new oak.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Pale, spicy and high-toned from bush vines on granite; a blending partner for Syrah and increasingly bottled alone.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: Old vines of the Cape's Hermitage, revived for light, fragrant reds and as the lifting part of a red blend.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre / Monastrell
grapes.styles: Dark, meaty structure for the red blends, well suited to the heat.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: Acid and bite from old vines, used sparingly in the red blends and occasionally bottled alone.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.styles: Old bush-vine Pinotage made in a lighter, whole-bunch style, far from the heavy oaked wines of the 1990s.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Apricot and perfume in the white blends, a small part beside Chenin, Clairette, Grenache Blanc and Roussanne.

grapes.name: Roussanne
grapes.styles: Waxy weight and length in the Rhône-style white blends.

law.classification: Swartland is a Wine of Origin district within the Coastal Region. The district carries wards that may be named on a label: Malmesbury, Riebeekberg, Riebeeksrivier, Paardeberg, Paardeberg South, Porseleinberg and, since 2022, Piket-Bo-Berg. Darling, to the west, was a ward of the Swartland until 2003 and is now a district of its own with the ward of Groenekloof. A stated ward or district must be true for every grape; vintage and variety need 85 per cent. The Swartland Independent Producers' charter of 2010 is a private standard, signalled by a small seal, and has no legal force; it is nonetheless the rule book that defines the district's style.
labels: The district, meaning black land, after the renosterbos shrub that darkens after rain.
Horse mountain, the granite dome on the Paarl border and a ward.
Porcelain mountain, the blue schist hill near Riebeek-Kasteel and a ward.
Castle mountain, the sandstone ridge above the Riebeek towns.
Coffee stone, the iron-rich ferricrete gravel found in the district's soils.
A marketing phrase unless the Certified Heritage Vineyard seal and a planting date back it up.
tiers: WO Coastal Region
The region that holds the Swartland together with Stellenbosch, Paarl, Franschhoek, Darling, Wellington, Tulbagh and Cape Town; a blend across districts falls back to it.
WO Swartland
The district label, true for every grape in the bottle, and the one most Swartland wines carry.
WO wards
Malmesbury, Riebeekberg, Riebeeksrivier, Paardeberg, Paardeberg South, Porseleinberg and Piket-Bo-Berg: a ward names a single hill or valley and is used by the single-site wines.
Swartland Independent Producers
A voluntary charter from 2010: Swartland fruit only, native yeasts, no added acid or tannin, a limit on new oak; a seal on the bottle, not a tier of law.
Certified Heritage Vineyard
The Old Vine Project seal, from 2018, for a vineyard of thirty five years or more, with its planting date; much of the Swartland's old Chenin qualifies.

made.viticulture: The Swartland's claim rests on the bush vine, planted without wires and left to its own shade, dry farmed on winter rain. Many Chenin, Cinsaut, Grenache and Pinotage blocks date from the 1960s to the 1980s, and from 2018 the Old Vine Project's Certified Heritage Vineyard seal has let a producer print the planting date of any block of thirty five years or more. Yields are tiny, a few tonnes a hectare at best on the old blocks, because the vine sets what the moisture allows. Newer plantings of Syrah, Mourvèdre and the Rhône whites are often trellised, but the growers who set the style have kept to bush vines and to the poorest ground, the granite of the Paardeberg and the schist of the Riebeek and Porseleinberg hills. Harvest is early and fast, from late January, with the sugar watched closely because the heat can outrun the flavour; picking slightly early for freshness is the house habit. The hazards are drought, which in a dry year can halve a crop, wind and sunburn; rot is seldom a worry. The wheat land around is sprayed and ploughed, so the vineyard's own cover crops and organic or biodynamic farming matter here more than in most Cape districts.
made.winemaking: The district's winemaking is a manifesto as much as a method, written down in the charter of the Swartland Independent Producers in 2010: wine from Swartland fruit only, fermented with the vineyard's own yeasts, with no added acid, no added tannin and only a small share of new oak, so that the place shows rather than the cellar. Reds are fermented with a large portion of whole bunches, trodden or punched down by hand in open vats, concrete or old wood, with little extraction, and aged in old barrels, foudres or concrete eggs; blends are assembled late, in the manner of the southern Rhône. Whites are pressed whole bunch, fermented on their solids in old oak or concrete and left on the lees for months, which gives the waxy texture of the white blends. Chenin is kept dry and unoaked in flavour, even where it spent a year in wood. Skin-contact whites and pét-nat have a following in the district too, but the exam cares for the Syrah blends and the old-vine Chenin.

places.name: Malmesbury
places.note: The district's main town and a ward in the shale country at its heart, home of the large co-operative cellar founded in 1948 that long absorbed the district's crop, and of the Sadie Family cellar on the Paardeberg side.

places.name: Paardeberg
places.note: The granite mountain in the south, shared with Paarl, whose Swartland face is the ward of Paardeberg with Paardeberg South beside it. Coarse decomposed granite, old bush-vine Chenin and Cinsaut, and the cellars that led the district's revival; its wines are perfumed, taut and mineral.

places.name: Paardeberg South
places.note: The ward on the southern flank of the mountain, warmer and more exposed, with the same granite and its own cluster of small cellars.

places.name: Riebeek-Kasteel and Riebeek West
places.note: Two villages under the Kasteelberg in the east of the district, the centre of the Swartland wine route, with Mullineux at Riebeek-Kasteel and the old estates at Riebeek West that once sent fortified wine and Shiraz to the whole country.

places.name: Riebeekberg
places.note: The ward on the Kasteelberg's slopes above the villages: shale and sandstone, cooler air with height, structured Syrah and Chenin.

places.name: Riebeeksrivier
places.note: The ward on the lower ground along the Riebeek stream, warmer and heavier in soil, with old bush vines on clay loam over shale.

places.name: Porseleinberg
places.note: A hill of hard blue schist near Riebeek-Kasteel and the ward named for it, where a Franschhoek house planted Syrah on the stones; its wine is the district's most famous single-site red, firm, graphite-edged and slow.

places.name: Piket-Bo-Berg
places.note: A ward gazetted in 2022, on the high plateau of the Piketberg in the district's north, with cooler nights and sandstone soils; its name means above the Piketberg.

places.name: Darling and Groenekloof
places.note: West of the Swartland towards the Atlantic, Darling was a Swartland ward until 2003 and is now its own district, with Groenekloof as its ward: cool sea breezes and sharp, green Sauvignon Blanc rather than the Swartland's reds.

places.name: St Helena Bay and the West Coast
places.note: The Berg River meets the Atlantic here at the district's north-western corner; a cool, windy coastal strip with a few vineyards, better known for the Benguela current's fishing than for wine.

producers.name: Sadie Family Wines
producers.why: The Malmesbury house whose Syrah-led Columella and white blend Palladius, from 2000 on, turned the Swartland from bulk land into a fine wine district.

producers.name: Mullineux
producers.why: The Riebeek-Kasteel house founded in 2007 whose single-soil Syrahs, Schist, Granite and Iron, teach the district's geology in three glasses.

producers.name: AA Badenhorst Family Wines
producers.why: A Paardeberg farm making textured white blends, Cinsaut and Grenache from old bush vines in old wood and concrete.

producers.name: Porseleinberg
producers.why: The schist-hill Syrah farmed by the Franschhoek house Boekenhoutskloof, the Swartland's single-site benchmark.

producers.name: Allesverloren
producers.why: The old Riebeek West estate, on a farm granted in 1704, that kept Shiraz and Cape port styles alive through the co-operative years.

producers.name: Lammershoek
producers.why: A Paardeberg estate whose old Chenin and Pinotage bush vines fed several of the revival's early wines.

producers.name: Swartland Winery
producers.why: The Malmesbury co-operative of 1948 that still bottles much of the district's volume and shows what the land made before the revival.

terroir.climate: Warm to hot Mediterranean, among the driest of the Cape districts: winter rain of roughly 300 to 500 millimetres, a long rainless summer and ripening days that pass 30 degrees. The Atlantic is near enough on the western side for afternoon breezes to reach the Paardeberg and the Darling hills, and nights cool sharply, which keeps acidity in grapes that have seen a great deal of sun.
terroir.soils: Two parents, read from any Swartland label. The Paardeberg is a dome of Cape granite that weathers to coarse, sandy, mineral-poor soil with pockets of clay; its wines are tense and perfumed. The Riebeek hills and the land around Malmesbury sit on Malmesbury shale and schist, which weather to heavier, iron-rich clay loams; their wines are deeper and more savoury. Porseleinberg's blue schist is the hardest and stoniest of all. Koffieklip, an iron-rich ferricrete gravel, turns up on both.
terroir.topography: Rolling wheat land between 100 and 300 metres, broken by three landmarks: the Paardeberg in the south on the Paarl border, the Kasteelberg above Riebeek-Kasteel and Riebeek West, and the Piketberg to the north. Vines take the slopes and the foot slopes of these hills, where the soil is poorer and the air moves; the plain between is grain and sheep.
terroir.water: The Berg River runs north through the district's eastern side on its way to the Atlantic at St Helena Bay, but most Swartland vineyards see no irrigation at all: the old bush vines are dry farmed on the winter rain their deep roots can find, and that habit is the district's identity.

traps: Swartland is a district, not a region: it sits within the Coastal Region, and a blend of Swartland with Stellenbosch fruit falls back to Coastal Region or Western Cape.
Skurfberg, the famous old Chenin site, is in the Citrusdal Mountain district of the Olifants River, not in the Swartland, though Swartland houses bottle it.
The Paardeberg is shared: the Swartland side is the ward of that name, with Paardeberg South beside it, and the Paarl side is the ward of Voor Paardeberg.
Darling and Groenekloof are no longer Swartland; they have been a district and its ward since 2003.
The Swartland Independent Producers seal is a private charter; the only legal guarantees are the Wine of Origin seal's origin, vintage and variety.
Swartland Syrah is savoury and medium bodied; expect pepper and fynbos, not the jam and oak of a hot-climate Shiraz.

wines.note: Medium-bodied, dark-fruited and peppery, with dried herb, olive and a stony finish; firm tannin, little or no new oak. Serve at cellar temperature with lamb, duck or anything off the braai.
Syrah led, with Grenache, Mourvèdre, Cinsaut and Carignan in the southern Rhône manner; savoury, lifted and built to age. Columella is the wine the exam names.

Dry, full in texture, with quince, baked apple, honey and beeswax over bright acidity and a saline edge; a wine for roast chicken, pork belly and rich shellfish. Many carry the Certified Heritage Vineyard seal with a planting date.
Chenin Blanc with Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Viognier, Roussanne or Sémillon, fermented and aged in old oak or concrete; waxy, nutty, long and dry, the Cape's answer to a white Châteauneuf.
Pale, red-fruited, lightly chilled wines from old Cinsaut and Grenache, poured by the glass with charcuterie and spiced dishes.
The Riebeek West estates long made fortified wine from Portuguese varieties under the Cape Vintage and Cape Tawny names, alongside sturdy Shiraz; the older face of the district.
wines.style: Cape port styles and Shiraz from the old estates

exam: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay: the Hemel-en-Aarde is the Cape's reference for both, with Hamilton Russell (1975) the founding name.
Hemel-en-Aarde means heaven and earth; it names three wards: Valley, Upper Valley and Ridge, in order inland from the sea.
Walker Bay is the district, in the Cape South Coast region, with seven wards including Bot River.
The climate: cool maritime, cold Walker Bay, the summer south-easter, low yields from wind at flowering.
The soils: clay-rich Bokkeveld shale in the lower valley, more decomposed granite inland.
Hermanus places it: south-east of Cape Town on the coast, famous for whales.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The valley's red: red and dark cherry, earth, spice and a fine, firm tannin; the Cape's most Burgundian reds.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Taut, citrus and stony, barrel-fermented with restraint; the Hemel-en-Aarde's other benchmark.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Bright, cool, flinty wines from the district's broader farms around Bot River and Stanford.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.styles: Lighter, fresher, more perfumed Pinotage from cool coastal sites, with red fruit in place of smoke.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Peppery, medium-bodied wines from the warmer Bot River farms.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: Old vines around Bot River give rich, textured, quince-and-honey Chenin.

law.classification: Walker Bay is a Wine of Origin district in the Cape South Coast region. It holds seven wards: Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley and Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge in the heaven-and-earth valley itself, with Bot River to the west, Stanford Foothills and Springfontein Rim to the east around Stanford, and the small Sunday's Glen. Hemel-en-Aarde is therefore not one appellation but the shared name of three wards; the atlas name Walker Bay / Hemel-en-Aarde joins the district to its famous valley. A ward name on the label means every grape grew in that ward; Walker Bay means the district; Cape South Coast or Western Cape covers wider blends. Vintage and variety need 85 per cent. There is no grape restriction and no ranking of sites.

made.viticulture: The Hemel-en-Aarde is trellised Pinot Noir and Chardonnay country, planted fairly densely, with vertical shoot positioning and rows set to cope with the south-easter. Wind at flowering is the great hazard: it disrupts fruit set and leaves small, loose bunches, so yields are naturally low and swing sharply from vintage to vintage. The cool, dry, windy summer keeps fungal disease down, though a wet spring can bring mildew. Virus in old plant material was an early problem across the Cape, and replanting with clean vines and better Burgundian clones has lifted the valley's wines. The shale holds water, so many blocks are dry farmed or lightly irrigated. Baboons and birds take their share where the vineyards meet the fynbos. Harvest begins with sparkling base wine and runs from February into March, later on the inland wards than near the sea. Growers pick for acidity as much as sugar, and the best farms work in small blocks matched to shale or granite.
made.winemaking: The Burgundian model rules. Chardonnay is whole-bunch pressed, fermented in French oak barrels with a modest share of new wood, often with native yeast, and aged on its lees before bottling; some houses restrain malolactic conversion to keep acidity. Pinot Noir is destemmed or fermented with a portion of whole bunches in small open vats, often after a cool soak, punched down by hand and aged in French oak, again with restrained new wood. The houses prize site and bottle single-ward or single-vineyard wines, so the Valley, Upper Valley and Ridge names appear prominently on labels. Sauvignon Blanc from the wider district is fermented cool in steel, and Cap Classique follows the traditional method with its second fermentation in bottle. Hamilton Russell's discipline, bottling only Pinot Noir and Chardonnay under the estate name, set the valley's tone.

places.name: Hemel-en-Aarde
places.note: The heaven-and-earth valley behind Hermanus, divided into three wards that climb inland from the sea. Together they are the Cape's answer to the question of where its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay grow best.

places.name: Hemel-en-Aarde Valley
places.note: The ward nearest the sea, a few kilometres from Hermanus, on stony, clay-rich Bokkeveld shale. Hamilton Russell Vineyards and Bouchard Finlayson are here, and it is the valley the exam means first.

places.name: Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley
places.note: The middle ward, farther from the sea, where decomposed granite mixes with shale; Newton Johnson is its best-known house, known for perfumed, site-specific Pinot Noir.

places.name: Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge
places.note: The ward farthest inland, on the high ground at the head of the valley, with shale and granite soils; Creation is among its houses.

places.name: Bot River
places.note: The westernmost ward, around the village of Bot River on the road to Elgin, warmer than the valley and on shale soils; old Chenin Blanc, Pinotage, Shiraz and Rhône grapes from houses such as Beaumont and Gabriëlskloof.

places.name: Stanford Foothills
places.note: Vineyards on the foothills of the Klein River mountains near the village of Stanford, east of Hermanus beyond the Klein River lagoon.

places.name: Sunday's Glen
places.note: A small ward inland of Hermanus, and one of the least seen names on a label.

places.name: Springfontein Rim
places.note: A small ward in the Stanford country south-east of Hermanus; a name to recognise on a label rather than to study.

places.name: Hermanus
places.note: The town on the bay, a fishing village turned resort, famous for southern right whales seen from its cliffs in winter and spring; the valley's wineries lie just behind it.

places.name: Cape Agulhas
places.note: The separate district to the east along the coast, around Africa's southernmost point, where the Atlantic and Indian oceans are conventionally divided. It is a neighbour of Walker Bay, not part of it.

places.name: Elim
places.note: The ward of the Cape Agulhas district near the southern tip: windswept, maritime Sauvignon Blanc, white blends and Shiraz from the southernmost vineyards in Africa.

producers.name: Hamilton Russell Vineyards
producers.why: Founded in 1975 in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, it proved the Cape could make serious Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and bottles only those two under its own name.

producers.name: Bouchard Finlayson
producers.why: An early Hemel-en-Aarde Valley house founded with Burgundian partners, for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

producers.name: Newton Johnson
producers.why: The Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley family house for perfumed, site-specific Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Creation
producers.why: A Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge estate known for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

producers.name: Storm Wines
producers.why: A Pinot Noir specialist bottling a separate wine from each of the three Hemel-en-Aarde wards.

producers.name: Beaumont
producers.why: The Bot River family farm known for old-vine Chenin Blanc.

producers.name: Southern Right
producers.why: Hamilton Russell's sister label for Pinotage and Sauvignon Blanc from the district.

terroir.climate: Cool maritime: the vineyards of the lower valley lie only a few kilometres from Walker Bay, and the cold sea and the strong summer south-easter keep afternoons fresh and the season long. Rain falls mostly in winter; summers are dry and windy, which limits disease but can disrupt flowering and cut yields. Moving inland and up the valley, the sea's hold weakens a little and days warm, but the wards stay among the coolest in the Cape. The wind is hazard and gift together: it keeps rot away and gives small berries with thick skins.
terroir.soils: The lower Hemel-en-Aarde Valley lies on Bokkeveld shale, weathering to a stony, clay-rich soil that holds water and gives Pinot Noir its structure and Chardonnay a firm line. Farther up the valley decomposed granite becomes more common, sandier and better drained, and growers find more perfume and a lighter frame in its wines. Table Mountain sandstone forms the ridges above. The contrast between shale and granite is the valley's own debate, argued block by block.
terroir.topography: The Hemel-en-Aarde runs inland from the coast just west of Hermanus as a narrow valley between mountain ridges, climbing from near sea level to higher ground on its upper reaches and the ridge beyond. The three Hemel-en-Aarde wards follow that climb: the Valley nearest the sea, the Upper Valley next, and the Ridge farthest inland. Bot River lies to the west, below the Houw Hoek pass that leads over to Elgin, and the Stanford wards lie to the east towards the Klein River lagoon and beyond.
terroir.water: Walker Bay, an inlet of the cold South Atlantic between Hermanus and Gansbaai, anchors the climate: its sea breeze reaches the lower valley every afternoon, and southern right whales come into it to calve in winter and spring. The Klein River lagoon east of Hermanus and the Bot River lagoon to the west are the other waters along this stretch of coast.

traps: Hemel-en-Aarde is not a brand or a single appellation; it is three wards inside the Walker Bay district.
Walker Bay is in the Cape South Coast region, not the Coastal Region.
Bot River belongs to Walker Bay, though it lies on the road to Elgin.
Elim is a ward of the separate Cape Agulhas district; its Sauvignon Blanc is not Walker Bay's.
The Hemel-en-Aarde's Pinot Noir is the Cape's most Burgundian red, but Pinotage, not Pinot Noir, is the national signature red.
Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley is the middle ward; the Ridge lies farthest inland.
The course line about the Atlantic at Walker Bay is right: the bay lies west of Cape Agulhas, where the two oceans are conventionally divided.

wines.note: Medium-bodied, with red cherry, raspberry, forest floor and spice over fine, firm tannin and bright acidity; the best age well for a decade. Serve slightly cool with duck, quail, salmon or mushroom dishes.
Citrus, white peach, hazelnut and a chalky, saline finish, fermented in French oak with restraint. Pour with lobster, crab, roast chicken or veal in cream.
Cool, flinty and citrus, with less tropical fruit than warmer Cape sites; for oysters, line fish and salads.
A lighter, more perfumed Pinotage of red fruit and gentle spice, far from the smoky, heavy style; good with grilled meats and spiced dishes.
Old-vine Chenin with quince, honey and texture from the warmer, shale-rich ward west of the valley; for pork, poultry and rich fish.
Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from the inland wards make fine, high-acid bottle-fermented sparkling wine; serve as an aperitif or with shellfish.
